source: Parpart, Schulz, Gershman, Yeung-Jacobs (2018) Heuristics as Bayesian inference under extreme priors
finding: Reanalysis of the 20 ABC data sets. Take-the-best beats linear regression only when training data are very small. Intermediate-strength priors beat both extremes.
numbers: 20 data sets (Czerlinski 1999): 3 to 18 cues, 11 to 395 objects, 55 to 77,815 pair comparisons, mean cue correlation 0.31. House prices: TTB beats regression at 20 training pairs (about 9% of 231); the order reverses at 100 pairs (about 43%). Half-ridge model: intermediate prior best on all 20 data sets at every training size (10, 20, 115 comparisons; 1,000 splits).
quote: ignoring information is rarely, if ever, optimal
limits: Models, not people. The half-ridge model assumes cue directions are known, so it shows no less-is-more; the authors say this is why.
agent_relevance: The TTB advantage is a small-sample effect. For S0 this means: a direct rule should be preferred when examples or class history are few, and a richer estimate once the class record grows. S0 needs a sample-size trigger.

source: Parpart, Schulz, Gershman, Yeung-Jacobs (2018) Heuristics as Bayesian inference under extreme priors
finding: With cue direction unknown (COR model), a less-is-more effect appears: tallying and TTB beat full regression at tiny training sizes. TTB wins in more data sets than tallying.
numbers: At 10 and 20 training cases, tallying beats regression in 11 of 20 data sets; TTB beats regression in 18 of 20. The tallying limit prior (1/eta^2 = 1,000,000) is beaten by full regression.
limits: Simulation on the same 20 data sets, so the environments are the original authors' choice. No new human or LLM data.
agent_relevance: Supports a sample-size boundary condition: simplicity wins when estimating from under about 20 cases. Our per-class pass-rate records start tiny, so S0 should lean on simple class priors early.

source: Parpart, Schulz, Gershman, Yeung-Jacobs (2018) Heuristics as Bayesian inference under extreme priors
finding: Heuristics are the limit of an infinitely strong prior. They win because strong inductive bias fits many real environments, not because simplicity is cheap or special.
numbers: Conclusion across the 20 data sets: an intermediate prior that uses all data generally beats a pure heuristic.
quote: ignoring information is rarely, if ever, optimal
limits: Theoretical framing. It rivals the claim that frugality itself is the cause of good performance.
agent_relevance: For design, prefer a shrinkage estimate (blend a simple prior with observed class data) over a hard switch between simple and complex modes.

source: Hogarth & Karelaia (2003/2007) Take-the-best and other simple strategies: why and when they work well in binary choice
finding: Take-the-best is effective across many environments with 3 to 5 binary cues, but hybrids of equal weights and TTB do better as environments become more compensatory. With error, TTB barely beats a naive rule that only exploits dominance.
numbers: Expected accuracy of the dominance-plus-random baseline: 84% (3 cues), 77% (4 cues), 71% (5 cues). In the 4-cue world 54% of distinct pairs involve dominance. Real data sets: TTB accuracy above 90% in theory, but with error TTB beat the dominance baseline by only 3 to 4 points (baseline averaged 68%).
limits: Binary cues, 3 to 5 cues, theory plus simulation plus real data sets. Error level is a key parameter.
agent_relevance: Hard boundary condition: when evidence is noisy, a simple rule gains little over a minimal baseline. Direct mode must be measured against a simple baseline, not only against deep reasoning.

source: Hogarth & Karelaia (2003/2007) Take-the-best and other simple strategies: why and when they work well in binary choice
finding: TTB is exactly 100% correct only when weights are non-compensatory and cue order is right. Wrong cue order costs a lot, and noise pushes every model toward chance.
numbers: TTB 100% with the non-compensatory weight function; equal-weight (EW) 86% and 89% in non-compensatory cases; the EW/TTB hybrid is strong in compensatory worlds. With medium error, accuracy fell toward 50% to 70% for all models (simulation, 100 repeats of 50% samples).
limits: Simulated populations with set weights. Real-world cue orders are estimated, not known.
agent_relevance: Direct mode depends on a good cue order, that is, a good class record. A stale record should lower trust in the fast path.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a decade of research
finding: Authors' own account of the recognition heuristic. Origin was serendipity: US students scored slightly higher on American cities than on German ones, a less-is-more effect. They stress the heuristic is for inference from memory and applies only when recognition validity is high.
numbers: Goldstein 1997: about 60% of US students right on Detroit vs Milwaukee, against 90% of German students. BBC 2009 informal replication: 65% right in New York, 82% in London.
limits: Written by the founders; the BBC test was uncontrolled. Universality is disowned in their Misunderstanding 1.
agent_relevance: Shows the boundary clearly: the rule is valid only in domains where the cue (here recognition) correlates with the criterion.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a decade of research
finding: Table of studies: adherence to recognition rises with recognition validity and falls when validity is low or unknown.
numbers: Examples: ski resorts mixed with cities 75% to 89% adherence; NHL career points (validity .87) 96%; disease frequency (validity .62 and .60) 64% and 71%; U.S. cities (validity .90) 95%.
limits: Table is compiled by the heuristic's authors. Many cells are single studies.
agent_relevance: Adaptive use: people fit the rule to validity. An agent can imitate this by gating the fast path on a measured validity of the cue.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a decade of research
finding: Collective recognition forecasts sports well. Wimbledon 2004: lay recognition beat ranking systems and replicated in 2005.
numbers: Recognition 72% correct vs ATP Entry Ranking 66%, ATP Champions Race 68%, expert seedings 69%. Scheibehenne & Broder (2007) found basically the same for Wimbledon 2005. Amateur players predicted the recognised player in around 90% of cases.
limits: Single sport, few tournaments. Authors first suspected a lucky strike.
agent_relevance: A cheap crowd signal can beat expert models. Links to Crowd within and ensemble work; not proof for LLMs.

source: Gigerenzer & Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a decade of research
finding: Evidence for noncompensatory use in individuals: many people choose the recognised option on every trial even when up to three cues point against it.
numbers: Pachur et al. 2008 and Pohl 2006: about half of participants (46% to 60%) chose the recognised object every time with 3 negative cues. Marewski et al. 2010: most voters always followed recognition; five compensatory models all predicted worse than the recognition heuristic.
limits: Aggregate adherence still falls when negative cues are added (for example 98% with positive cues to 81% to 67% with negative ones in one study). No fitted process model of the minority is known.
agent_relevance: Individual differences are large. An agent that treats all inputs the same loses the fit; per-class strategy choice is the analog.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler, Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Adherence to recognition in lab tasks is high but depends on validity across environments.
numbers: About 90% of choices in geographic comparisons; 89% for US students on German cities, 71% of them correct; NHL: 95% chosen, 87% correct. Across 11 environments mean adherence correlated with mean recognition validity, r = 0.64, p = 0.03. Individual level: r = -0.03.
limits: Correlation rests on 11 environments. Individual validity did not predict individual adherence.
agent_relevance: Environment-level fit is clearer than person-level fit. Calibrate S0 gating on class-level statistics, not on a single run.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler, Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Direct tests of noncompensatory processing show a mixed picture: strong in some labs, weaker in others.
numbers: Goldstein & Gigerenzer 2002: 92% stayed with recognition against learned cues. Richter & Spath 2006: median 97%, mean 82%; 17 of 28 mostly followed. Newell & Fernandez 2006: aggregate 64%, 23% of people always followed. Hilbig 2010: 62% to 76% noncompensatory.
limits: Different designs: cues learned in lab vs from memory, and different cue counts. Critics say averaging hides individual strategy.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the 'ignore other cues' claim holds for a subset of people and in some designs only.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler, Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Source and criterion knowledge override recognition. When the recognition did not come from the world, or the criterion is known, people stop using it.
numbers: Mixed reference class: adherence fell from 89% to 75% (Pohl 2006). Known nearly-eradicated disease: the unrecognised one was judged more frequent in 85% of cases. Recognition caused by the experiment: about 30% to 37% recognised choices (Oppenheimer).
limits: Compiled from several studies.
agent_relevance: S0 should check why a cue is available. A cue that comes from the prompt itself (like experiment-induced recognition) is not evidence about the world.

source: Pachur, Todd, Gigerenzer, Schooler, Goldstein (2011) The recognition heuristic: a review of theory and tests
finding: Less-is-more is supported mainly by simulation, and the evidence in real data is mixed.
numbers: Across 10 data sets (Pachur 2010) the effect is mixed and shrinks when knowledge validity rises with the number of recognised objects. Katsikopoulos 2010 showed the effect can arise even when recognition validity does not exceed knowledge validity.
limits: Review by heuristic proponents.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'knowing less is better' as a design claim for the agent.

source: Pohl (2011) On the use of recognition in inferential decision making: an overview of the debate
finding: Independent critic's audit of the less-is-more effect: most demonstrations are simulations; empirical ones are weak.
numbers: Maximum theoretical effect 26.3% (recognition validity 1.0, knowledge validity .50). Goldstein & Gigerenzer 2002 counted a 0.3% difference as a slight effect without a test; a second study found 3.5% with induced recognition, later criticised even by the authors. Snook & Cullen data: picking two individuals shows an effect; picking the two with most recognised shows 'more-is-more'.
limits: Pohl is a critic, but gives concrete counts.
agent_relevance: Less-is-more claims need a regression over many people, not a selected pair. The same rule applies to our own per-mode comparisons.

source: Pohl (2011) On the use of recognition in inferential decision making: an overview of the debate
finding: Rival process models fit people better than the toolbox: parallel constraint satisfaction and evidence accumulation.
numbers: Glockner & Broder (2011): 77.5% of participants best fit by compensatory PCS, up to 7.5% by recognition heuristic. Newell & Lee (2010), using a minimum description length criterion, found a sequential evidence-accumulation model, with TTB as a special case, fit best.
limits: Fit depends on task: 'givens' tasks give compensatory models an edge; memory-based tasks give TTB more.
agent_relevance: The adaptive toolbox is not the only account. The same behaviour may come from one flexible integrator. Do not build S0 on the claim that people switch tools.

source: Glockner & Broder (2011) Processing of recognition information and additional cues: a model-based analysis
finding: Maximum-likelihood strategy classification (choices, response times, confidence) finds few recognition-heuristic users when cue values of the unknown object are shown.
numbers: 83 students took part. 77.5% best fit by PCS (compensatory); recognition heuristic (enhanced) up to 7.5%; take-the-best 15%. Excluding one PCS version still gave 73% to 74% PCS users. Confidence and time predictions were significant for PCS but not for RH or TTB. 120 city-size comparisons.
limits: Cue values were shown, not retrieved from memory; founders argue this is outside the heuristic's domain.
agent_relevance: Challenge to 'people use one-reason rules'. Behavior that looks like a heuristic can come from a compensatory process.

source: Glockner & Broder (2014) Cognitive integration of recognition information and additional cues in memory-based decisions
finding: Follow-up in which cues had to be retrieved from memory: the compensatory model still wins, but non-compensatory use rises.
numbers: 62% of participants best fit by PCS; 32% classified as RH or TTB users (up from 22.5% before). Cue learning reached 90% correct for the average participant; 61% hit the 90% criterion. PCS predicted 73% of choices, RH and TTB 71%.
limits: Single task (US city size) and one lab. Effortful retrieval is the moderator.
agent_relevance: Cost of retrieval is a moderator: when information is expensive to get, one-reason rules appear. This matches a token-budget argument for direct mode.

source: Bobadilla-Suarez & Love (2018) Fast or frugal, but not both: decision heuristics under time pressure
finding: Frugal is not the same as fast. When told to use take-the-best, people were slower and complied less than with tallying under time pressure in one design; the order reversed in another.
numbers: Experiment 1: 206 recruited, 179 analysed; 26.26% of the TTB group excluded. Heuristic x time pressure on compliance F(1,177) = 329.37; on RT F(1,177) = 313.50. Experiment 2: 194 recruited, 173 analysed; interaction F(1,171) = 135.95 for compliance, tallying slower. 2,000 ms deadline.
quote: TTB, however frugal, can be slow
limits: Participants were instructed which heuristic to use; GDP cues were artificial; online sample.
agent_relevance: Fewer cues does not mean lower cost. For the agent, measure real tokens and steps; a one-cue rule may need an ordered search that is not cheap.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annual Review of Psychology
finding: Take-the-best beats three complex learners in cross-validation across most training sizes, in the founders' simulations.
numbers: Compared with nearest neighbour, C4.5 and CART on city size and mammal longevity (Brighton & Gigerenzer 2011); TTB higher at most sample sizes and in most of 20 environments. Estimated cue orders from samples of two to ten still gave TTB higher accuracy than regression (Katsikopoulos et al. 2010).
limits: Figures only; exact percentages not in the review text I read. Founders' lab results.
agent_relevance: Complex flexible learners overfit tiny samples. Same logic as few-shot calibration of an LLM mode switch.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annual Review of Psychology
finding: Fast-and-frugal trees matched logistic regression in prediction across 30 classification problems, and beat it in an emergency room.
numbers: Martignon et al. 2008: 30 problems, trees close or identical to logistic regression in prediction, worse in fitting. Green & Mehr 1997: doctors sent about 90% of chest-pain patients to ICU though only about 25% had infarction; the tree beat the 50-probability logistic instrument and nearly halved false alarms.
limits: Field results are from a small number of hospital or court studies; effect sizes in the review are qualitative.
agent_relevance: A short ordered checklist is a real tool for direct mode with a stop rule, and is auditable.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annual Review of Psychology
finding: Heuristics can be better than a state-of-the-art model in business and law.
numbers: Hiatus heuristic (inactive if no purchase for 9 months) 83% correct vs Pareto/NBD 75% for one firm; airline 77% vs 74%. Bail decisions (Dhami 2003): trees 92% and 85% correct in two courts vs 86% and 73% for a weighted additive model, but the tree ignores due-process information. Stroke bedside exam: 100% sensitivity, 96% specificity vs MRI 88% sensitivity.
limits: The legal tree predicts what magistrates do, not what is right. Stroke sample had 25 non-stroke patients.
agent_relevance: A heuristic can predict human behaviour well and still be a bad norm. Check what the target is before copying a simple rule.

source: Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier (2011) Heuristic decision making, Annual Review of Psychology
finding: Stated boundary conditions: one-reason rules do best when uncertainty and redundancy are moderate to high; individual differences make group-mean tests misleading.
numbers: Cited: Hogarth & Karelaia 2007 for uncertainty, Dieckmann & Rieskamp 2007 for redundancy. 1/N: parental time in 1,296 families matched the 1/N prediction that middle-born children get least time (Hertwig 2002).
limits: Review without new data.
agent_relevance: Use as S0 features: noise level and cue redundancy of the task class.

source: Brighton & Gigerenzer (2015) The bias bias
finding: Argues that researchers overweight bias and underweight variance when comparing simple and complex models. Seen only as a search-result summary.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; summary from search snippets only.
agent_relevance: Variance term is what simple rules cut; ties to the sample-size boundary in the first lines.

source: DeMiguel, Garlappi, Uppal (2009) Optimal versus naive diversification: how inefficient is the 1/N portfolio strategy?
finding: Out-of-sample, none of 14 optimising models consistently beat equal allocation in Sharpe ratio, certainty-equivalent or turnover.
numbers: 14 models, 7 data sets (10 in the 2005 working paper). Mean-variance would need about 3,000 months of data for 25 assets, about 6,000 for 50, to beat 1/N.
limits: Not opened; from search snippets only. Per-model numbers not seen.
agent_relevance: Clear finance case where estimation error beats optimisation. Same variance logic as the Bayesian reanalysis.

source: Dana & Dawes (2004); Nelson (2018, Vanderbilt thesis) The superiority of simple alternatives to regression
finding: Dana & Dawes found equal or correlation weights usually predict as well as regression in social science. A 2018 partial replication found that within a plausible parameter range the gap differs from their report, but still advises against abandoning OLS except with strong prior knowledge.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Not opened; abstract-level only. Nelson says the 2004 result had not been replicated before his work.
agent_relevance: A rare independent re-test of the 'simple weights' claim; shows the claim depends on parameter range.

source: Katsikopoulos, Schooler, Hertwig (2010) The robust beauty of ordinary information
finding: Simulation over 19 environments: TTB with estimated cue order does well even from very small training sets; intuited cue directions in 10 environments performed about as well as order learned from 50% of the objects.
numbers: 19 environments; 10 with elicited intuitions.
limits: Not opened; abstract-level summary from search results.
agent_relevance: Answers the 'hidden complexity' objection: a cheap, noisy order can be enough.

source: Newell & Shanks (2004) On the role of recognition in decision making
finding: Early critique: people use more than recognition when they know why an object feels familiar. Known only via later citations.
numbers: No figures read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports the source-knowledge check described for the Pachur review.

source: Bogdan (2026) Free energy heuristics: fast-and-frugal cognition as active inference under uncertain precision
finding: Only direct LLM test found: extended chain of thought lowers accuracy on high meta-uncertainty items, which the author reads as take-the-best-like truncation. No arm tests TTB itself.
numbers: 7 models (5 open-weight 3B to 32B, 2 frontier), 5 CoT lengths (none, about 3, 7, 15 steps, unconstrained), 7,875 responses, 5 replications per cell, FEH-79 benchmark (79 items, confirmatory subset 45). Accuracy drop 17.3 points in the high regime (95% CI 7.7 to 25.5); matched definite-answer items showed no cost.
limits: Single-author preprint (June 2026); pre-registered gate cleared. Strong in mid-to-large models, directional in the two frontier models, absent or reversed in the weakest. Realised-step analysis reversed direction. Theory about TTB equivalence is not tested.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence that direct mode may beat long reasoning on unverifiable, high-uncertainty tasks. Not on our benchmarks, and the effect is model-dependent; test per class before use in S0.

source: Borro et al. (2025) Large language models as common-sense heuristics
finding: Not about fast-and-frugal rules. It uses LLM output as a search heuristic (hill-climbing) for planning.
numbers: Plans in a household environment: 22 percentage points higher task success than similar systems.
limits: 'Heuristic' here means a search guide, a different sense. Listed to avoid a false match.
agent_relevance: Low relevance to ecological rationality; do not cite as support.
